title: Why Gandhari tied the cloth
hookLine: a bride binds her eyes for her blind husband, and Hindus have argued about the pativrata ever since
carry: the devoted wife: honored, and questioned
tomorrow: The night the river gave back the dead
last: WHERE DHARMA IS, THERE IS VICTORY.

lines: A FEW LINES IN THE EPIC.
cards: Paintings show it. So do films and television. A strip of cloth, tied over Gandhari's eyes.
A princess of Gandhara learns that the prince she will marry, Dhritarashtra, is blind, and she binds her own eyes. The Mahabharata tells it in a few lines and moves on. Hindus haven't moved on.
Today: the cloth, the old ideal it stands for, and the honest argument about it.

teach.b: Here's what the first book of the Mahabharata gives, in paraphrase. Gandhari hears that her husband-to-be is blind. She takes a cloth, folds it over, and binds her eyes, resolving not to go beyond her husband.
The cloth is the most well-known picture of an old Hindu ideal: the pativrata, the wife wholly devoted to her husband. The epic takes that ideal seriously.
Its forest book has a whole section named for the greatness of the devoted wife, and Savitri's story, later this week, sits inside it.
And the tradition believed such devotion, kept like a vow, built real power, the same heat of self-discipline, tapas, that sages win in the forest. The epic shows it.

teach.h: BUT DHARMA ALSO NEEDS EYES OPEN
teach.b: After the war, when Yudhishthira bows before her, grieving and angry, Gandhari's eyes fall through a gap in the cloth onto his toes, and his nails turn dark.
Later retellings add that one look from her could have made Duryodhana's body hard as diamond. That's the ideal honored.
Now the question, and it's an old one too: a woman of clear sight chose not to look, at a court that badly needed someone to look, while her sons went wrong.
Many modern Hindus, and many devout ones, hold both: the devotion was real and powerful, and seeing clearly is part of dharma too.
That's why the ideal is still argued over in Hindu homes, around fasts wives keep for husbands, and why plenty of families now read devotion as something both partners owe.

how: Hindus meet Gandhari's blindfold in retellings of the Mahabharata on stage and screen, where it is held up as the devotion of a pativrata, a devoted wife; the same ideal stands behind fasts some wives keep for their husbands, and many Hindus today also question it.

a princess blindfolded by her father as punishment

it gives a few lines: she binds her eyes, resolving not to go beyond her husband.
the tradition believed a devoted wife's restraint built real power, like a sage's tapas
after the war, one glance through a gap in her cloth darkens Yudhishthira's nails.
all Hindus agree the blindfold is simply the right example to copy
it's honored as devotion and questioned too: dharma also needs eyes open.

games.q: a friend asks: was Gandhari's blindfold devotion, or a refusal to look? what's the honest answer?
o: only devotion. no one should ever question it.
both readings are real: the tradition honors the pativrata, and many ask whether she should have looked.
only a mistake. the tradition never honored it.
games.why: the epic honors her devotion and shows its power; readers, many of them devout, still ask what her sons lost when she stopped looking.

practice: If you're somewhere safe, close your eyes or rest a hand gently over them, and notice how the room changes: the sounds come closer, the body gets louder.

After a few breaths, bring to mind someone you're devoted to, and ask one quiet question: is there something about them, or about us, I've chosen not to see? Don't solve it now; just let your eyes open slowly.
If you pray, you can ask for devotion that sees clearly.

wordCard.voice: Gandhari. Hearing her husband was blind, she bound her own eyes, and became the epic's most well-known picture of the devoted wife, honored and questioned. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit, pativrata: one whose vow (vrata) is her husband (pati); the devoted wife.

carryVoice: Your line: the devoted wife, honored and questioned. Gandhari's cloth holds both. Until tomorrow.
